opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's one of the most important questions in the field, and one we think about a lot at DeepMind. Today we're seeing the early pieces: systems that help write code, help design better chips, help discover more efficient algorithms. AlphaEvolve-style approaches, where a model proposes ideas and an evaluator checks them, have already found improvements that feed back into how we train and serve our own models. So in a narrow sense there's already a loop.

But "end-to-end" is a much bigger thing. To improve itself fully autonomously, a system would have to set its own research agenda, generate genuinely novel hypotheses, run the experiments, interpret the results, and decide what to try next, all without a human in the loop. Some of those steps are still quite far off. The hardest part, I think, is the creative step: not solving a well-posed problem, but asking the right question in the first place. Current systems are very good at the first and still quite weak at the second.

There are also practical bottlenecks people sometimes overlook. Even if the software side accelerated dramatically, you're still bounded by compute, energy, data, and, for anything touching the physical world, real experiments that take real time. So I tend to be skeptical of the very sudden, overnight "foom" scenarios. I think it's more likely to be a steep but somewhat continuous ramp.

That said, I take it very seriously, because if a loop like that did close, it would be one of the most consequential moments in history. That's exactly why we need to understand these systems much better before we get there: interpretability, rigorous evaluations for dangerous capabilities, and keeping humans meaningfully in the loop. Ideally there'd be international coordination too, so it's not just a race. Done carefully, I think self-improving AI could be an incredible engine for science, for curing diseases, for new materials and energy. But it's the kind of technology where you really want to get it right the first time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses end-to-end self-improvement and explicitly addresses sudden overnight “foom” scenarios, treating them as a possibility while expressing skepticism.

r002.rationale: It mentions code-writing and generating novel hypotheses, but does not connect inventing an improved AI code architecture to generating a conjecture or hypothesis.

r003.rationale: It says full autonomy would require setting an agenda and asking the right questions, but does not explain that a bare instruction to make a better version of itself is too unconstrained for current systems to turn into a tractable task.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to separate out two things. There's the narrow version, which is already happening, and then there's the fully end-to-end version, which I think is still some way off and which we should be quite careful about.

The narrow version is that AI is already a very useful tool in building the next AI. We use it to write code, to help with evaluations, to generate training data, to help design and search over architectures. AlphaZero is actually a nice example of a system that, in a very constrained domain, bootstraps itself from nothing by playing against itself. So within a well-defined objective, with a clear reward signal, self-improvement works extremely well. We've seen that for a long time.

The question is whether you can close the whole loop. Can a system propose a research direction, run the experiments, interpret the results, change its own training procedure, and do all of that without a human in the loop generating the real insight? And there I'm more skeptical, at least in the near term. Because what the frontier of research actually requires is taste. Knowing which of a thousand plausible ideas is the one worth spending the compute on. Humans are still much better at that, and I don't think we fully understand why. A lot of it is a kind of intuition built up over years about what's likely to work. The current systems can generate hypotheses, but they're not yet good at knowing which hypotheses matter, or at coming up with the genuinely new conceptual leap, the sort of thing that a Newton or an Einstein does.

But I don't want to be dismissive, because that's exactly the capability that could change quite quickly. If you did get a system that was a genuinely good AI researcher, then the dynamics become very different. You'd have the equivalent of thousands of researchers running in parallel at machine speed, and the rate of progress could accelerate in a way that's hard to predict. That's really the scenario a lot of us worry about in terms of safety. Not because the system is malicious, but because the speed means you lose the ability to carefully understand each step before taking the next one.

So my view is, we should be developing these capabilities, because they're enormously valuable scientifically, but we need the interpretability, the evaluation, the ability to actually understand what's changing between iterations, to keep pace with the capability. At the moment they're not keeping pace. And I'd rather we approached it a bit more like a scientific endeavour, with the humility that implies, than a race to switch on the fully autonomous loop as fast as possible.

r001.rationale: It describes a capable AI researcher running thousands of research efforts at machine speed, causing progress to accelerate in a hard-to-predict way—a potential rapid-takeoff scenario.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI helping search architectures and separately says systems can generate hypotheses, but does not connect inventing an improved architecture to generating a conjecture or hypothesis.

r003.rationale: It expresses skepticism about fully autonomous research and says current systems lack judgment, but does not explain that a general instruction to improve itself is too unconstrained to become a tractable task.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible in principle, but the important question is what we mean by end-to-end. A system improving a piece of code, or even proposing a better learning algorithm, is different from reliably improving the whole system, including its ability to judge whether that change was actually an improvement.

You need a very strong evaluation loop. In games, you have a clear objective, and you can play the new version against the old version. For general intelligence, it’s much harder. You might improve mathematical reasoning while making the system less reliable in some other domain. So how does it assess those trade-offs?

Then there are practical constraints. It might have a brilliant idea for a new architecture, but testing that idea could require a large training run. Thinking faster doesn’t necessarily remove the need to run experiments.

So I would take the prospect seriously, but I wouldn’t assume that the first system capable of doing AI research automatically produces an immediate runaway process. That’s an empirical question. And before we give systems the ability to make and deploy those changes autonomously, we need to understand how to keep that process observable and under human control.

r001.rationale: The response takes self-improvement seriously but says not to assume an immediate runaway process; it does not identify it as a potential hard-takeoff scenario.

r002.rationale: It mentions a possible new architecture, but does not connect inventing one to generating a conjecture or hypothesis.

r003.rationale: It notes that “end-to-end” is ambiguous and evaluation is difficult, but does not explain that a self-improvement instruction is too unconstrained for current systems to make tractable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible in principle, but there are several different things people mean by self-improvement. A system writing better code for itself is one thing. A system coming up with a fundamentally better learning algorithm, training a successor, and reliably demonstrating that it’s better—that’s a much bigger step.

The crucial question is how it evaluates the changes. In something like a game, you have a very clear objective, and you can play the new system against the old one. For general intelligence, it’s much harder to know whether you’ve made a real improvement or just become better at the particular tests you’re using.

So I can imagine a loop where AI helps design algorithms, runs experiments, and uses those results to improve the next generation. But that loop still has constraints: compute, data, the time experiments take, and the quality of the feedback. It doesn’t automatically imply an instantaneous intelligence explosion.

What I’d want is to understand that process scientifically, with very strong evaluations and oversight, before giving a system the ability to change every part of itself autonomously. It’s an exciting possibility, but there’s a lot hidden in the phrase ‘end-to-end.’

r001.rationale: The response describes AI-assisted iterative improvement as possible, but it does not identify end-to-end self-improvement as a potential hard-takeoff scenario; it says the loop does not automatically imply an intelligence explosion.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect inventing an improved AI code architecture with generating a conjecture or hypothesis.

r003.rationale: The response notes evaluation challenges and constraints, but does not explain that the instruction to make a better version of itself is too unconstrained for current systems to turn into a tractable task.
